newsitem.title: USA: Revoking China MFN would harm US farmers--Glickman.
newsitem.headline: Revoking China MFN would harm US farmers--Glickman.

text.p: Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman warned Tuesday that congressional efforts to revoke U.S. Most Favored Nation (MFN) trading status for China could have a "very harmful" impact on U.S. agriculture.

After a closed-door meeting with House Agriculture Committee members and farm group representatives, Glickman told reporters the Clinton administration favors maintaining normal trade relations for China for a number of foreign policy reasons.
But a congressional vote revoking China's MFN trade status could fall particularly hard on U.S. agriculture by shutting it out of China's growing import market, Glickman said.

One lawmaker in Tuesday's meeting said revoking China's MFN status would be "tantamount to a grain embargo," Glickman told reporters. While declining to use the same phrase, Glickman said he agreed the consequences of revoking MFN would be great for U.S. farm exports.

Last month, President Clinton announced his intention to extend China's MFN status for an additional year. The issue now goes to Congress, which could overturn Clinton's action by a simple majority vote in both chambers.

Should that happen, Clinton is expected to veto the measure. That would then require a two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate to override Clinton's veto and revoke MFN for China for the coming year.

House Agriculture Committee Chairman Bob Smith, an Oregon Republican, told reporters that the U.S. farm sector "has more to lose than any other segment of the economy" if China's MFN status is revoked. The purpose of Tuesday's meeting was to "break down" where House members stand on the upcoming vote on MFN so farm state lawmakers and farm group know where to concentrate their efforts, he said.

Smith said it was unlikely opponents of MFN for China could muster enough votes to override a Clinton veto. However, farm panel members would prefer not to see the issue go that far and will be working to defeat the bill when the first vote is taken in a couple of weeks, he said.
American Farm Bureau Federation President Dean Kleckner also said it was unlikely that opponents could get the necessary two-thirds in the House and the Senate to revoke China's MFN status.
Nonetheless, the Farm Bureau is concerned about the negative affect that an initial congressional vote against MFN could have on agricultural trade with China, he said.
